title: Represent Fractions on a Number Line
goal: I can partition one unit into equal intervals and locate a fraction.
catchAll: The distance from zero to one is one whole. Count intervals from zero, not tick marks.

teacher.def: The denominator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are in the whole. It is the bottom part of the fraction
A unit fraction is ONE part of a whole. It always has a numerator of one.
The numerator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are being described. It is the top part of the fraction.
A fraction is a number used when a whole is split into equal parts.

glossary.whole: the one shape, unit length, complete piece or entire set named in the question
glossary.partition: divide a whole into equal parts
glossary.interval: the distance between neighboring marks on a number line

screens.title: Name the whole
text: One whole is the distance from zero to one.

screens.title: Connect the parts
text: Equal intervals represent equal unit fractions.
The distance from zero to one is one whole. Count intervals from zero, not tick marks.

screens.title: Check the reasoning
text: Count intervals from zero to locate a fraction.

item.prompt: Why do we count intervals instead of tick marks on a fraction number line? Write a complete sentence.
item.example: We count intervals because each interval is one equal part of the unit, while the first tick only marks where zero begins.
hints: Describe what the whole is and how its parts are counted.
show: Compare your reasoning with a grown-up or the model response.
We count intervals because each interval is one equal part of the unit, while the first tick only marks where zero begins.

options.text: Tick marks including zero.

options.text: Only the tick marks after the point.
options.why: The denominator comes from the whole unit, not what remains after the point.

items.prompt: A line has seven tick marks from zero through one, including both endpoints. How many equal intervals lie between them?

options.text: Eight intervals.
options.why: Count the spaces between neighboring marks.

options.text: Six intervals.
Seven intervals.
options.why: The two endpoints are boundaries, not additional intervals.

show: Seven boundary marks enclose six intervals.
items.yes: Compare your reasoning with the explanation.

items.prompt: The first interval on a unit line is longer than the others. Is counting four intervals enough to locate fourths?

options.text: No; all four intervals must have equal length.
Yes; the interval count alone is enough.
options.why: Equal interval lengths are part of the fraction model.

options.text: Yes; the longest interval always represents one-fourth.
options.why: A longer interval would represent a different distance.

show: Fourth-sized intervals must have equal lengths.
items.yes: Compare your reasoning with the explanation.

items.prompt: Which action places 2/3 on a line from zero to one?

options.text: Divide into two equal intervals and count three.
options.why: That reverses the numerator and denominator.

options.text: Count zero as the first interval.
options.why: Zero marks the start; no interval has been traveled there.

options.text: Divide the unit into three equal intervals and count two from zero.

show: Three tells the equal unit partition and two tells the traveled intervals.
items.yes: Compare your reasoning with the explanation.

items.prompt: A point is halfway through the unit. If the unit is divided into eight equal intervals, how many of those intervals lead to the point?

options.text: Four.
Eight.
options.why: Eight intervals reach the full unit.

options.text: One.
options.why: One interval would cover only one-eighth.

show: Four of the eight equal intervals cover half the unit.
items.yes: Compare your reasoning with the explanation.

items.prompt: A fraction point moves one equal interval to the right while the unit partition stays unchanged. What changes in its fraction name?

options.text: The denominator increases by one.
options.why: The denominator describes the fixed unit partition.

options.text: Both numbers must decrease.
options.why: The point is farther from zero, not closer.

options.text: The numerator increases by one; the denominator stays fixed.

show: An extra traveled unit part increases the numerator.
items.yes: Compare your reasoning with the explanation.

sections.heading: What your child is learning
sections.text: I can partition one unit into equal intervals and locate a fraction.

sections.heading: Ask for reasoning
list: Why do we count intervals instead of tick marks on a fraction number line?
What is the whole in this model? How do you know the parts are equal?
Can you explain the same idea with another picture or real objects?

sections.heading: Try it away from the screen
list: Make a paper number line. Keep equal spacing within each whole, and count intervals from zero.
Let your child explain a mistake before offering a correction.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Counting boundary tick marks instead of intervals.
Changing the whole halfway through a question.
